title: what a sikh carries and why
hook: what a Sikh carries and why
tomorrow: the tenth guru, the khalsa, the saint-soldier

segments.voice: Yesterday: chardi kala. Your line was rise anyway. Today, five things some Sikhs carry every day. Day eighteen.

A wedding ring turned during a hard meeting. A photo in a wallet. A grandmother's watch that doesn't keep time anymore. Small things people carry to remember. They don't do anything, exactly. Touch one, and something comes back: a promise, a person, who someone meant to be. Initiated Sikhs carry five of them, every day.
screen: `A RING, A PHOTO, A WATCH.` → `TOUCH IT, AND SOMETHING COMES BACK.` → `A SIKH CARRIES FIVE.`

segments.voice: They're the five Ks, because in Punjabi each one begins with the sound k. Sikhs initiated into the Khalsa, the family that began with the five on day four, keep all five. Kesh: uncut hair, from day three, under the turban. Kanga: a small wooden comb tucked into the hair. Keep the hair clean and ordered, and the life too. Kara: the steel circle on the wrist, also from day three. Kachera: a cotton undergarment, like simple shorts: self-restraint, and readiness to move. Kirpan: a small sword, worn in a sheath, often under the clothes. It stands for the duty to protect people who can't protect themselves, and for dignity and courage. It isn't there for aggression. Notice what all five have in common. None is a decoration. A comb, a bracelet, underwear, hair: plain, ordinary things. The reminders aren't locked away in a temple. They're on the body, at work, at the gym, all day. Faith you can touch. Many Sikhs who aren't initiated still wear the kara, and wherever you are with the rest, this path starts from there.
screen: `FIVE THINGS THAT BEGIN WITH K.` · `KESH AND KANGA — HAIR, AND ITS COMB.` · `KARA — THE HAND REMEMBERS.` · `KACHERA AND KIRPAN — RESTRAINT, PROTECTION.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you're wearing or carrying: a ring, a watch, a hair tie, your sleeve. Put your hand on it and decide, just for now, what it will remind you of: something you believe, a person, a promise. Close your hand around it and breathe with that meaning for a while.
The five Ks. Kesh, kanga, kara, kachera, kirpan: five reminders a committed Sikh carries every day. Eighteenth word.
Your line: reminders you can touch. Faith that goes where you go, not left behind at the door. Day eighteen.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: kakar, the name for the five articles of faith that begin with k.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh uniform.
what it means: five plain reminders, worn on the body every day: hair, comb, bracelet, undergarment, sword.
what a scholar hears: in Punjabi they're the panj kakar. the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, lists them as required for initiated Sikhs.
